drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Choose two. Which two situations should go to escalate to human? A,
drills.answer_line: SAM: The churn risk is real, and the anger needs acknowledging. But the
drills.stem: Which two situations should go to escalate to human?

options.A: On a routine return, the customer writes "I want a person, not a bot."
options.B: Refund wanted to a different card; refund policy says nothing about changing payment methods
options.C: Customer in capitals and swearing about a late parcel that qualifies for a standard refund
options.D: The agent rates its own confidence at 4 out of 10
options.E: Get customer returns 3 accounts matching the customer's name

drills.why: A is an explicit request: honour it at once. B is policy silence. C is within the agent's capability; D is self-reported confidence; E needs another identifier.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. A retail team's project CLAUDE dot md requires a shared error-handling
drills.answer_line: SAM: Miss pattern three. A is the first step: slash memory shows whether
drills.stem: A retail team's project CLAUDE.md requires a shared error-handling helper. In one package Claude keeps ignoring it, and developers say the behaviour differs between sessions. What should they do first?

options.A: Run /memory there to see which memory files are actually loaded
options.B: Restate the rule in capitals at the top of the project CLAUDE.md
options.C: Copy the rule into each developer's user-level CLAUDE.md
options.D: Add a hook that rejects any edit that skips the helper

drills.why: "First" and "differs between sessions": /memory shows whether the file is loading at all. B is louder guidance; D enforces before anyone has diagnosed.

drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Choose two. A public health research run produces reports whose claims
drills.answer_line: SAM: Both. Attribution was lost in the hand-off, so the hand-off has to
drills.stem: A public health research run produces reports whose claims carry no citations, although the web search subagent's results included URLs and dates. Which two changes fix the root cause?

options.A: Search and analysis subagents return claim-source mappings that synthesis must preserve and merge
options.B: Pass findings to synthesis as structured data keeping content separate from URLs and other metadata
options.C: Add "always cite your sources" to the report subagent's system prompt
options.D: Give the synthesis subagent web search so it can find the sources again
options.E: Move synthesis to a model with a larger context window

drills.why: Attribution was lost in the hand-off, so the hand-off has to carry it. C asks for citations the report agent no longer has; E cannot restore unpassed mappings.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Three hours into mapping a legacy insurance claims system, the agent
drills.answer_line: SAM: A. Talk of typical patterns instead of named classes is how the guide
drills.stem: 3 hours into mapping a legacy insurance claims system, the agent stops naming the classes it found earlier and says things like "services like this usually follow a repository pattern". What is the best change?

options.A: Keep a scratchpad file of key findings and consult it for later questions
options.C: Start a new session and have it read every file again
options.D: Add "be specific" to the system prompt

drills.why: Typical patterns instead of named classes is context degradation, and a scratchpad file keeps findings across that boundary. D asks for detail already lost.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. A bank's review bot posts findings, and developers dismiss about a
drills.answer_line: SAM: A. It turns dismissals into data you can count, which is the guide's
drills.stem: A bank's review bot posts findings, and developers dismiss about a third. The team wants to know which code constructs produce the dismissed findings, so they can fix the prompt for those. What should they add?

options.A: A detected pattern field on each finding, so dismissals group by the construct that triggered them
options.B: An instruction to report only findings the model is confident about
options.C: A move from synchronous calls to the Message Batches API
options.D: A free-text box where developers explain each dismissal

drills.why: It turns dismissals into data you can count. B is the confidence-filtering trap; C changes cost, not precision; D produces comments nobody aggregates.

drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. A logistics firm has three extraction tools: one for bills of lading,
drills.answer_line: SAM: A. Any guarantees a tool call and still lets the model choose the
drills.stem: A logistics firm has 3 extraction tools: bills of lading, customs declarations, delivery receipts. The type isn't known in advance, and sometimes the model replies with prose instead of calling a tool, which breaks the downstream loader. What fixes this?

options.B: Force the bill of lading tool on every request
options.C: Keep tool choice on auto and tell the model to always use a tool
options.D: Merge the three into one schema with every field optional

drills.why: Any guarantees a tool call and lets the model choose the right schema when several exist and the type is unknown. C is still probabilistic.

drills.question_line: SAM: Before the last word, your turn. Pause and name the six scenarios, and the classic trap
drills.answer_line: ALEX: Customer support, escalating on sentiment or self-rated confidence.
drills.prompt: Name the six scenarios, and the classic trap in each.
drills.answer: Support: sentiment or self-rated confidence. Code: user-level rule. Research: wrong agent blamed. Dev tools: reading every file. CI: "be conservative". Extraction: required field for absent info.

In this episode: Read a scenario frame and know what it rules out
Support, code generation, research, productivity, CI, extraction
The 3 decisions each scenario keeps probing
The classic trap in each scenario
6 patterns that run through all of them
The frame and customer support: Glance at the left-column frame every item; reread when it changes
Frame constraints: 80% first-contact resolution, minimise false positives
Support: order that must hold lives in code, prerequisite or hook
Escalation triggers: explicit request, policy gap, no progress
Multiple matches: ask for another identifier
Case facts block, trimmed lookups, structured escalation summary
Scenario two: code generation: Team-wide config in project scope; personal in the home folder
Scattered file types: rules file with a paths glob
CLAUDE.md always loaded; skills on demand
Skill frontmatter: context: fork, allowed-tools, argument-hint
Plan mode for many files or approaches; direct for a clear single fix
Trap: a rule that lives in someone's user-level file
Scenario three: multi-agent research: Coordinator decomposes, partitions, selects subagents, loops on gaps
Task in allowed tools; several Task calls in one response for parallel work
Subagents inherit nothing; 4 or 5 tools per role
Structured claim-source mappings; structured error context
Conflicting credible sources: keep both, annotate, coordinator reconciles
Trap: blaming a subagent when the coordinator's decomposition is the cause
Scenario four: developer productivity: Grep for contents, Glob for paths; Edit fails, Read then Write
Build understanding step by step from entry points
Better MCP tool descriptions; catalogues as MCP resources
Community servers for standard integrations like Jira
Subagents, /compact, resume with changed files, fork to compare
Scenario five: continuous integration: -p / --print runs unattended; JSON output with a schema
CLAUDE.md supplies testing standards, fixtures, review criteria
Explicit categories and few-shot output format; disable a noisy category
Per-file plus integration passes; prior findings on re-runs
Blocking checks synchronous; overnight work to Message Batches API
Trap: "be conservative"; independent instance beats self-review
Scenario six: structured extraction: Extraction tool with an input schema removes JSON syntax errors
tool_choice auto, any or named; nullable fields, "unclear", "other"
Semantic checks: calculated total beside stated total
Retry with document, failed extraction and specific error
Batch: 50% off, 24h, resubmit failures by custom_id; segment accuracy
Trap: a required field for information that may be absent
Patterns across scenarios: What must happen every time lives in code
Specific beats general; confidence counts only when calibrated
Absence and failure get honest values
Scope follows audience: team in the project, personal at home
Recap: the exam tells: Support: asks for a person, escalate at once; only angry, resolve; rule must hold, hook or prerequisite
Code generation: behaviour differs between sessions, /memory first; single file, direct; dozens, plan
Research: narrow report, coordinator's decomposition; vanished citations, claim-source mappings
Productivity: typical patterns instead of named classes, scratchpad; Jira, community MCP server
CI: same session reviews its change, independent instance; unknown dismissals, detected_pattern field
Extraction: unknown type and prose back, tool_choice any; value in another document, null or review
Glance at the left column every item: the frame often settles the item
